newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia likely to import wheat - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia likely to import wheat - analysts.

text.p: Yugoslavia will have to import wheat this year despite government assurances of adequate domestic supply, analysts said on Thursday.
Yugoslavia, comprising Serbia and Montenegro, used to export wheat, but one industry expert said this year's record low crop would not feed the country swollen with war refugees.
"Yugoslavia will have to import wheat this year," said Slobodan Stepanovic, secretary to the Association of Agricultural Cooperatives from the wheat-region of Vojvodina.
Most analysts and officials declined to comment, although privately they conceded that the government's wheat stockpiles were lower than it admits, and inadequate for needs.
"The farmers who harvested 70 percent of the wheat crop are unwilling to sell it to the state," said Stepanovic. "They do not trust the government any more."

In the worst harvest in two decades, Yugoslavia reaped 1.72 million tonnes of wheat this year with a yield of 2.96 tonnes per hectare. State cooperatives produced about 500,000 tonnes and private farms about 1.2 million.
According to official estimates, Yugoslavia needs at least 2.5 million tonnes of wheat each year.

Federal Agriculture Minister Tihomir Vrebalov said this year's harvest, along with the last year's stock, would meet domestic demand. But he admitted the government has banned wheat exports to avoid the need for imports.
Belgrade plans to buy 631,000 tonnes of wheat from farmers, exchanging half for fuel, fertiliser and seed, and the rest in cash installments. It has so far purchased 122,000 tonnes.
Serbian farm cooperative expert Tihomir Madic said most farmers were reluctant to accept the relatively low state price of 0.90 dinars per kilo.
"Farmers are exchanging only the minimum quantity necessary for their autumn sowing and cattle breeding," he said.

Agriculture Ministry official Milan Prostran said farmers had stored but not sold some 300,000 tonnes of wheat, adding he expected the state to purchase a million tonnes of wheat from this year's harvest.

Farmers' spokesman Stepanovic said only nine percent of this year's wheat harvest from Vojvodina has been sold to the state. "It is a drastic fall compared to over 90 percent sold to the government last year," he said.
Stepanovic blamed low wheat sales on the reduced harvest and the government's poor record of payments to farmers.
Madic said there was enough wheat in the country to feed the people, but "farmers keep it in attics. They will gradually sell it or exchange it...it will be a very slow process."
